newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end off, Fed remarks weigh on market.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end off, Fed remarks weigh on market.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower Tuesday, dragged down by remarks by a Federal Reserve official saying the consensus at the central bank appears to be centered around a 25 basis-point rate hike in September.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at the day's lows at 30/32 at 96-18/32. Its yield jumped sharply to 7.03 percent from 6.95 percent at Monday's close.
Analysts said the comments prompted many to shift their expectations on what the Fed will do at its September 24 meeting to a possible tightening from an unchanged policy.
"The market is in the process of shifting back to looking for a 25-basis-point hike (in September)," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
The Fed official told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that there is a consensus at the central bank emerging "around a 25-basis-point increase in the funds rate."

The official, who asked not to be named, also said eight of the 12 district banks in the Fed system have requested a hike in the 5.0 percent discount rate amid mounting evidence growth is likely to remain brisk in the second half of 1996.

The votes favoring a higher discount rate were taken at various regional Fed board meetings in recent weeks. Bank board meetings are held at a regular basis, but the schedules differ from bank to bank.
"We saw some good selling on the story right off the bat; across the curve we saw selling," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at CS First Boston Corp.
Although the sentiment in the market appears to have become more bearish, some analysts said they have maintained their view that the Fed will not raise rates in September.

"Our call for the Fed is no change ... for the entire year in fact," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities. She added that the sell-off on Tuesday had not changed her mind "at all" about what the Fed will do next.
The heavy selling, however, prompted many to dump long positions in the short-end of the curve, sharply narrowing the spread between the 30-year bonds and the two-year notes.

The flattening of the curve put the spread between the two securities at 77 basis points from 83 points on Monday. "The short-end dropped sharply as people re-evaluated their positions," a trader at a U.S. bank said.
Analysts said day-traders, dealers and speculators were very active throughout the day. Some corporate-related selling was also cited as a factor weighing on prices.
Chart analysts, who had predicted last week that any rise in prices should be considered a rally in a bear market, said the selling Tuesday was already expected.
"Charts had indicated the market was growing a little bit overbought," said a dealer who trades mostly on charts.
I.D.E.A.'s Stiles said he sees bond yields, currently around 7.0 percent, moving higher to 7-1/8 and then 7-1/4 percent over the next three weeks or so.
Analysts said the market mostly shrugged off news that August industrial production jumped 0.5 percent against a 0.1 percent rise in July. Capacity utilization was 83.5 percent.

Market also paid little attention to the release of a 0.1 percent drop in retail sales in the first two weeks of fiscal September versus August as measured by the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook index.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up 11 basis points at 5.17 percent. The six-month bill rate was up eight points at 5.27 percent. The year bill rate rose 10 points to 5.53 percent.

The two-year note closed off 8/32 at 99-24/32, yielding 6.26 percent. The five-year note traded down 17/32 at 99-16/32 to yield 6.62 percent. The ten-year note closed down 24/32 at 101-6/32, yielding 6.83 percent.
